nodes.question: Which groups are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of the challenges mentioned in water, energy, and food management?
nodes.answer: Low- and middle-income states are particularly susceptible to these impacts.
nodes.paragraph: Water, energy and food resource management faces challenges such as limited accessibility, increas- ing demand and risks from the international market. Considering an anticipated global population of about 9 billion by 2050, food and energy production are expected to increase by 70% and 50%, respectively, while water demand will increase by 55%. Half of the global population is predicted to experience water stress by 2050 (UNDP, 2015). Limited access to land and water will lead to trade- offs and competition between food and energy production. These challenges have been exacerbated by the pandemic, with directly impacts on both water and food contamination, and indirectly effects unemployment, social unrest and disrup- tions in supply chains. Low- and middle-income states are particularly suscepti- ble to these impacts (Diffenbaugh et al., 2020). Studies highlighted the vulnerabilities and gaps in the existing systems and proposed strategies for enhancing resilience and sustainability in the face of simi- lar future crises (Cheshmehzangi, 2020; Deaton & Deaton, 2020). The pandemic served as a wake-up call for the importance of integrated approaches to address the interdependencies between the water, energy and food segments.

nodes.question: What has caused doubt among a significant portion of the population about climate change?
nodes.answer: Doubt about climate change has been caused by the perception that scientific evidence is often unconvincing, alongside various socio-political and psychological factors.
nodes.paragraph: Vol. :(123456789)Environmenta Chemistry Letters (2025) 23:363 366 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-24-1800-9 EDITORIAL Connecting records of global to regional climate John P . Jasper1 Eric Lichtfouse2 Published online: 9 December 2024 The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 It S just weather. It S just natural cycles. It S not an exact sci - ence. It S a hoax Despite the accumulating scientific evi- dence supported by numerous facts and observations span- ning many decades, a substantial portion of the population doubts the observations that demonstrate the human causes of climate change. This hesitation may arise from the fact that scientific evidence often does not convince them and, indeed, research has shown that skepticism about the exist- ence, the causes, and the consequences of climate change derives from socio-demographic features, political ideology, and psychological factors [1 ]. Here we summarize cogent data connecting global-to-regional climate change based on the levels and isotope compositions of atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1000 AD, the global temperature anomaly since 1880 AD, and the average Connecticut air tempera- tures since 1896 AD.
